articles.text: Piedmont High School’s Class of 2026 celebrated with a lively graduation ceremony on Thursday, June 4, at Witter Field. Their commencement ceremony honored their accomplishments and welcomed family, friends, and teachers to witness their last gathering together before heading into the world in separate directions. This special class is heading for greener pastures. The matriculation list shows a whopping 15 students committed to Cal Berkeley, and 48 in total heading directly to a University of California site. PHS graduates will be represented at three Ivy League schools, as well as Stanford, Northwestern, Washington University in St. Louis and the University of British Columbia to name a few. These students finished the 6th grade remotely due to Covid and some were reunited with their 6th grade teacher Ted Scherman, the high school commencement speaker. He finished his speech with wise words of advice that offered perspective to the graduates: “Be kind to your parents. This moment is enormous for you. But it is everything to them,” PHS graduates assemble for one last time as a class at their graduation ceremony.

articles.text: Every year, we gather in May at the PHS amphitheater to celebrate senior athletes who go on to compete in college. They set an example for younger athletes who hope to follow in their footsteps. But the landscape is shifting so quickly that last year’s template may not work next year. We’ve seen college roster sizes shrink, eligibility rules change, and donors pour money via NIL to bolster their schools. At the pre-college level, we’re seeing an equally interesting shift: private equity firms are injecting capital into youth club teams, showcases, and facilities. KKR has influence within the soccer ecosystem including programs such as MLS NEXT and ECNL. 3STEP has acquired dozens of soccer, lacrosse, volleyball, basketball, and softball organizations nationwide. And many of the facilities these organizations use operate under agreements with companies backed by PE firms such as Unrivaled Sports. Here’s the kicker: the coaches influenced by these organizations sit at the top of the pecking order when it comes to influencing teenage athletes. They’ve convinced kids to give up other sports or risk falling behind. They’ve convinced athletes that the next pay-to-participate showcase will be the one that gets them recruited. They minimize practice—the time when athletes develop their skills—and replace it with more and more games. The result? Families spending thousands of dollars for their kids to become perpetually injured from overuse, all while doing the opposite of what college coaches want: developing skills and demonstrating adaptability by succeeding in multiple sports. More info: 94% of NCAA athletes across Divisions I, II, and III played at least two sports growing up, and 84% played two sports at the varsity level. Simply put, if your goal is to play a sport in college, you’re more likely to succeed if you play multiple sports. To summarize: if you’re exceptional at one sport, sure, you’re talented. But if you’re good at a second sport, it’s a differentiating factor. It’s your way of proving you’re self-motivated, are coachable, have a broader set of skills, and may be less susceptible to overuse injuries. The landscape of college sports will continue to evolve, and I can’t pretend to know what the future will hold. But it seems clear to me that the combination of club coaches, ChatGPT, social media algorithms, and vibes isn’t as reliable as simply asking college coaches themselves and trusting the people who genuinely care about you. Pouyan Assadi is the varsity head coach of the Piedmont High School track and field team, and the JV head coach of the PHS football team.
articles.title: A not-so-subtle shift in youth sports

articles.text: In April earlier this year Camp Augusta’s director Randy Grayson, announced that this summer would be his last in the role. Grayson spent the last 23 years at Camp Augusta building the camp into an internationally respected summer residential camp for kids. Grayson is expected to remain involved with Augusta, participating in family camps, training, and running story experiences. As a kid, summer camps helped Grayson gain self-confidence, social skills, independence, creativity, physical and leadership skills. As an adult, he spent his time trying to give that experience to future generations, spending the last three decades working on his mission. Going into his final summer, Grayson is excited that he no longer has to worry about logistics and can focus on the hands-on experience with the kids. He plans to become a grandparent who gets to do all the “fun stuff.” “I’d like to be engaged with the program in the community, and kind of flip it in the way that I have the time to spend more time with the campers and the staff, and do the clinics,” Grayson said. “I hope that this transition is a time when I can do more of what I love at camp, rather than answer 50 emails and talk about things like the food truck and budgets.” When Grayson arrived 23 years ago, the camp was $5 million in debt and required significant repairs. He was contemplating whether to stay or leave on a month-to-month basis. Ultimately, what kept him involved with the camp was the passion he observed in the people dedicated to preserving it. Randy Grayson with his family “A couple of years before I got there, they started to try and run a camp program again, where the camp actually ran for several weeks, half full, but they still were trying to make a go of it, to have it there. The camp had a candle; it wasn’t dead, it still had a flame,” said Grayson. The Camp Augusta board allowed Grayson and his staff to shape its culture. In his first year running the camp, it was 80% full and was able to run the entire summer. For the next 22 summers, the camp has been full. Having full enrollment and donors enabled the camp to rebuild its infrastructure. As Grayson steps away, he hopes he provided the kids with a sense of possibility and a belief that they can try new things. Through the camp’s playstations and evening embers, he wanted to encourage campers to try new activities and discover what they want and what they like. After collecting his final thoughts, Grayson thanked those who had attended Camp Augusta throughout his 23 years with hopes the camp continues to grow and thrive in future years. “I am delighted to leave Camp Augusta in a really strong place organizationally. We’re glad to be full every year and have a strong financial base. I hope Augusta continues to rise and grow in ways that I probably wouldn’t have imagined,” said Grayson. Grayson’s next step is to dedicate time to his nonprofit organization, A Meaning of Life. The organization’s goal is to provide resources to help people practice positive habits and improve their lives. Readers and Camp Augusta fans can find Grayson’s nonprofit at the following link: https:// ameaningoflife.org/. Randy Grayson gave a speech to the campers before the traditional oatmeal fight.
articles.title: Randy Grayson’s final summer at Camp Augusta

She wants to be part of whatever is going on, likes to stay close to people, and has a soft little meow she uses to ask for attention. This sweet girl loves to play: toys are a favorite, but she’s always happy to keep an eye on any flies that might wander indoors. Tiki can become over-excited during play and may swat if she gets carried away, so she’ll do best with someone who can read her body language and recognize when playtime is over. Randy Grayson with his family “A couple of years before I got there, they started to try and run a camp program again, where the camp actually ran for several weeks, half full, but they still were trying to make a go of it, to have it there. The camp had a candle; it wasn’t dead, it still had a flame,” said Grayson. The Camp Augusta board allowed Grayson and his staff to shape its culture. In his first year running the camp, it was 80% full and was able to run the entire summer. For the next 22 summers, the camp has been full. Having full enrollment and donors enabled the camp to rebuild its infrastructure. As Grayson steps away, he hopes he provided the kids with a sense of possibility and a belief that they can try new things. Through the camp’s playstations and evening embers, he wanted to encourage campers to try new activities and discover what they want and what they like. After collecting his final thoughts, Grayson thanked those who had attended Camp Augusta throughout his 23 years with hopes the camp continues to grow and thrive in future years. “I am delighted to leave Camp Augusta in a really strong place organizationally. We’re glad to be full every year and have a strong financial base. I hope Augusta continues to rise and grow in ways that I probably wouldn’t have imagined,” said Grayson. Grayson’s next step is to dedicate time to his nonprofit organization, A Meaning of Life. The organization’s goal is to provide resources to help people practice positive habits and improve their lives. Readers and Camp Augusta fans can find Grayson’s nonprofit at the following link: https:// ameaningoflife.org/. articles.text: At the June 1 City Council meeting, council members agreed they want to place a measure increasing the property transfer tax rate on the November ballot. City staff is expected to prepare a draft of the ordinance to read at the council’s next meeting on June 15. At this time, the council is undecided on the exact number for the proposed increase; discussions will continue at the next meeting. The City Council requested that the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee examine funding mechanisms to address the city’s deferred maintenance obligations, capital infrastructure needs, and long-term revenue sustainability. The advisory recommended that the council consider increasing the transfer tax by either a flat or tiered rate. The recommendation was a range between 1.5% and 1.8%. According to the financial planning committee, A rate adjustment, if approved by voters, would provide a more durable source of capital funding and reduce the General Fund’s dependence on volatile annual transfer tax receipts for capital investment. The council agreed with the budget advisory committee’s recommendation to raise the property transfer tax. The increasing costs of maintenance and capital investments have prompted the city to explore ways to increase revenue. “It’s our streets, our sidewalks, our storm water drains, it’s this infrastructure that’s aging that’s getting more expensive because the cost of everything is going up, and our revenues are not matching that,” said Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen. The council could not reach a consensus on an appropriate amount to increase the transfer tax. However, they agreed to a flat-rate increase due to the volatility associated with a potential tiered system. “The transfer tax is a very volatile revenue source, and adding a tiered structure makes it even more volatile. It’s anybody’s guess as to how many large value properties are going to sell, so it becomes even harder to project revenue,” said Finance Director Kiran Bawa. In Piedmont, the transfer tax has been unchanged for the last 33 years at a rate of 1.3% or $13 per $1,000 of assessed value. The city uses the funds from the transfer tax toward capital investment and maintenance of aging facilities, buildings, and infrastructure systems. The city attempted to increase the transfer tax in 2020 with Measure TT, which would’ve increased the rate to $17.50 per $1,000 of assessed value, generating an estimated $948,462 per year for city services. The measure was defeated, with 52% voting no. Six years later, the council still believes that there is a need for an increase to help balance the city’s revenue. “The need has not gone away; the need we had in 2020 is the same. In fact, maybe we have a better understanding of the need six years later,” Mayor Andersen continued. “We were cushioned over those six years by having two bumper transaction sales years that filled up the coffers of our capital needs funds, but those were outlier years, and those are not years that we’re going to repeat anytime soon.” If the council places the transfer tax measure on the November 2026 ballot, measure materials would need to be submitted to the Alameda County Registrar of Voters no later than August 7, 2026. Discussions on the potential increase of the transfer tax will continue at the council’s next meeting on June 15. Readers who wish to attend the meeting can do so in person at City Hall or online. More information is on the City’s website: https://piedmont.ca.gov/.

articles.text: Ted Scherman, now a retired middle school teacher, was the Commencement Speaker at Thursday’s Piedmont High School Graduation Ceremony. Class of 26, it is truly an honor to be your commencement speaker today. And in a way, I’m graduating right along with you. This is bittersweet for me, this is my swan song, and I am overwhelmed with gratitude that John Morrison - yes, of the John Morrison Gym - tracked me down 32 years ago and offered me a job. To the parents: It has been a privilege to teach your children. They are remarkable in more ways than I can count. I have taught so many kids over the years, and each one has a place in my heart. And sometimes I hear from former students, and they’re married, with children of their own. I have even taught the children of former students. What?! Graduates, I know so many of you here today. Some I had in class, some in an elective, and some through sports. And some of you, I honestly cannot believe you made it. All kidding aside, this is a distinct honor, and I thank you for asking me and for allowing me to dispense some completely unsolicited advice on this year’s graduating class. For me, the Class of 2026 will always hold a special place. Six years ago, I had the pleasure of welcoming so many of you to Piedmont Middle School, whether it was during the Welcome to 6th Grade Bootcamp, or in one of my 6th grade classes. I remember watching you adjust, find your footing, and begin to thrive. And then, just as you were hitting your stride, everything stopped. Covid shut it all down. And while we all managed somehow, I never got to say a proper goodbye to you. So here it is. Finally. Goodbye, 6th graders. Hello, graduates. I want to take a moment to congratulate you, genuinely, deeply, on making it to this point. I’m not sure everyone in this room fully appreciates what it took. Let’s go back. Elementary school. You were nervous. Will I make any friends? Will the teachers be mean? Am I going to miss my mom and dad? You rocked tetherball and were fierce on the four-square court. Ready to bring your skills to middle school. Then middle school. Even scarier. No recess? You mean we’re just supposed to stand around and look cool? What do you mean it’s not okay to wear my Winnie the Pooh t-shirt anymore? What happened to my friend, and why are they acting so weird? Then high school. The pressures shifted again. How do I stand out? Why is my friend taking five AP courses? Will any college accept me? Can I go to that party? What if I don’t want to go? It’s a lot. The pressures are real and should never be discounted. And now, look at you. Here you are. You’ve done it. Before I get to my advice, take a moment right now. Look up at the stands. Find the parents, grandparents, siblings, coaches, teachers, scout leaders, religious leaders, mentors, and every person who believed in you. Send them a silent, telepathic thank you. Because none of us goes at it alone. Everything you have achieved, and will achieve, is a combination of your own perseverance and the support of so many people. You’ve spent the last 3, 7, 10, 15 years here in this village. This hamlet. This cocoon. This nest known as Piedmont. It is a very special community, and whether you know it now or will come to know it later, you were well cared for here. Now it’s time to move on. To leave the nest. I’ve sat through a few graduations in my time, so trust me, I’ll keep this short and sweet. Three things. Just three. First: Play Play with abandon. Play until your sides hurt from laughing. At some point, kids stop playing, and I want to ask you: when did YOU stop? Games, fun, harmless pranks, playfulness with friends, a spontaneous game of tag, play is how we communicate, how we learn about one another, and how we find levity when life gets too real. It is also, frankly, a lot of fun. It’s so good for you, and for everyone around you, to be reminded not to take ourselves too seriously. Even animals in the wild maintain playfulness their whole lives – with their offspring, with their mates. When we lose that childlike quality, we lose sight of something really important. Very few jobs are life or death - unless you become a surgeon, in which case, please take that one seriously. When you move to a new town or city – and many of you will, find the rec league. Join the acting troupe. Find the outdoors club. PLAY DODGEBALL! Create the conditions for play, and the playfulness that’s been dormant inside you will push right through. Ultimately, the reason play is my number one piece of advice is simple: the joy it brings to anything you do. Play allowed me to enjoy 32 years with pre-adolescents. Imagine what it can do for you. Second: Be curious Be curious about whatever interests you. Be curious about yourself, about your loved ones, about your studies, about the world. Put the phone down. Get off YouTube and Instagram, find a trail nearby, leave the phone at home, and just go. Be curious about where your mind wanders when you let it. Most of you have no idea what you want to do when you “grow up.” Curiosity can lead you somewhere worth going. The last thing I ever imagined being was a teacher. But I got curious about it, and my dad kept saying, Teddy, you should be a teacher, and here I stand, 32 years later, giving a high school commencement speech to a community full of people I love. And one more thing about curiosity and this new chapter: you’re embarking on an adventure. The thing about adventures is that you never know what they’ll actually be like. You may have a vision. You may have heard from others what college or work or life in a new city will be like. But it won’t be that. It will be wonderful, and unpredictable, and at times, lonely and hard. Don’t be fooled by other people’s social media. While you’re sitting alone, wondering what’s wrong with you, someone else’s Instagram feed will make it look like they are surrounded by their besties and couldn’t be happier. Remember: that’s a curated moment in time. It is not reality, and comparison is the thief of joy. It takes a long time, real time, to make a true friend. Be patient with yourself. Curiosity brought me here. Let it take you somewhere wonderful. Third: Be kind to your parents This moment is enormous for you. But it is everything to them. In the blink of an eye, you went from a toddler strapped into a swing, being pushed up, up, up into the air, giggling with delight, to driving a car, which is terrifying, to sitting here today in a cap and gown. Be loving to them. Their lives exploded with love the moment you came along. You busted open their hearts in a way they never thought possible. And now, you’re leaving… I don’t think many of you remember Dutch, that was my first love. A chocolate lab. When my wife was expecting our first child, I remember thinking: how can I possibly love anything more than I love Dutch? It’s just not possible. Then Lucas came. Then Julian. Then Quincy. And my heart was forever altered, with a love that was both fiercely protective and endlessly expansive. Every parent in this room would do anything for you. Anything. So call them. Tell them thank you. Tell them you love them. Do it today, not someday, and do it regularly. Congratulations, Class of 2026. Go play. Stay curious. And call home. Thank you.

articles.text: PHS Valedictorian Nathan Tuan will be attending the University of California, Los Angeles in the fall of 2026. Good evening everyone—principals, teachers, families, friends, and most importantly, the graduating class of 2026. Graduates, we happen to be sitting in alphabetical order. Parents, you happen to be sitting in places of your own choosing. So, here’s the question: would you rather have assigned, or unassigned seating? Hold onto that thought while I tell you a story. My first memory of Piedmont High School was when I transferred here in 10th grade. On opening day, I walked into Mr. Palsa’s classroom at 8:15 a.m. After I introduced myself, he prompted me to find my seat. There was a piece of paper with a hand-drawn diagram of our seating arrangements. It was like hieroglyphics to me. I stumbled around sitting in one wrong seat after another, Mr. Palsa shaking his head each time, until I finally found the right one. A year passed. Through assigned seating charts, I built new friendships with the people I coincidentally ended up near. Our shared challenge in classes like Honors Chemistry and APUSH were incubators for meaningful relationships. When I asked you all that question, most people would probably answer unassigned. There’s comfort in deciding where to sit, who to sit with, and where you belong. But if there’s anything I learned these short, intense 3 years, it’s to keep yourself open to uncertainty. Be okay sitting with new people and trying out new things, because the freedom we have in choosing our own seats may be the very thing that restricts our horizons. Sometimes we have to sit in all the wrong seats to know when we’ve found the right one. An added bonus about leaving things to chance is that it can lead to pleasant surprises—I met Niko and Timmy in elementary school, but we separated in middle school when they transferred away. For a long time, I never had the chance to reconnect with Niko until just this year, when we happened to be in the same classes, and seated right next to each other. We picked up right where we left off. Now, he’ll be giving a speech right after mine, quite literally picking up where I leave off. So, assigned or unassigned seating? Whichever life gives you, have the courage to sit in every seat until you’ve found the right one. Class of 2026, congratulations on graduating. Thank you.

This is the highest rank in Scouts BSA, the Scouting America (formerly Boy Scouts of America) program for 11 to 17 year old youth. Lorrel Plimier, a City Councilmember representing Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, prefaced a City Proclamation with these remarks: “Our society, our world, survives because of people like Eagle scouts who are willing to serve their communities, and willing to be leaders in their communities. And this is as important now, or even more so, than it has ever been. “As young women also, you are setting an example for young girls who come behind you. And this may seem like a small thing, but I can guarantee you it’s not. It is very important. “No matter where you end up, the world needs more people like you.” Sarah King, Troop 4 Eagle Mentor, reminded fellow scouters, families, and friends, about the audacity of having women join the ranks of Eagle Scouts: “2019 was the beginning of a new era in Scouting as girls were finally welcomed into the Scouts BSA program. In Piedmont, four girls – Camille, Mollie, Lizzy, and Naomi – became members of the first female troop. If you look closely at Naomi’s uniform, you’ll notice that she wears the Founder’s Bar, which signifies that she joined Troop 4G during its inaugural year. Of those four original founders, three have now achieved the rank of Eagle Scout.” Naomi’s scouting journey started in February 2019 at Troop 406G’s (girls) open house in Sunnyvale, just days after Scouts BSA officially admitted girls. When the family decided on a move to Piedmont at the end of February, Naomi was comforted Piedmont Council Registrar Laural Fawcett (left), Troop 4 Former Scoutmaster Jeroen Grasman, and Troop 4 Eagle Scout Andrew Grasman Troop 11 Eagle Scout Isabelle Myers Troop 4 Eagle Scout Naomi Treichler Troop 4 Summer Camp Coordinator Stacy Lau (left), former Scoutmaster Walter Stokes, Assistant Scoutmaster Angela Anastasi, Eagle Mentor Sarah King, Merit Badge Counselor Kimery Leong, Tenderfoot Scout Henry Gross, and Advancement Chair Anna Kneitel Master of Ceremonies and Troop 11 Eagle Scout Theo Ferguson (left), former Troop 4 Scoutmaster Walter Stokes, former Troop 11 Scoutmaster Tom Smegal, Naomi Treichler and Isabelle Myers Piedmont Council Scouting America Scout Executive Tess English (left), Troop 11’s Martin Crawford-Jakubiak, City of Piedmont Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, and Jennifer Ferguson of Troop 11 in learning that Piedmont troops would also welcome girls in what was eventually a remaking of all Piedmont troops into co-ed units. Seven years later, Naomi submitted her Eagle application before her 18th birthday. Despite Naomi’s reserved nature, she truly enjoyed connecting with a larger community of scouts from troops outside Piedmont while at summer camp and outside the United States at the 2023 World Scout Jamboree in South Korea. Naomi joined scouting for the fun activities as soon as she could and stayed in Troop 4F (family) as its Senior Patrol Leader in 2023. “In that role” explained King, “the SPL serves as the bridge between the Scouts and the adult leadership while also running troop meetings. I think it’s fair to say this role pushed Naomi outside of her comfort zone. Imagine standing here every Monday night trying to get a room full of mostly middle-school boys to stop talking, stand quietly, and listen to the agenda. It wasn’t easy. But over time, Naomi found her voice. She learned how to rely on her composure and preparation to lead effectively. It would have been tempting to walk away, but she didn’t. In doing so, she taught the Scouts an important lesson about leadership: it isn’t always loud, but it is persistent.” In another pocket of Piedmont, Isabelle joined Troop 11 in May 2023. Isabelle’s less conventional story, started in her freshman year of high school, is an equally impressive rise through the scouting ranks on a shorter timeline and with a much busier schedule. Unlike the meandering approach to scouting of most middle school students, Isabelle had Eagle rank in her sights, and she set a very direct path to that end Scouting is all about allowing youth to set their own goals, with trusted adults providing the necessary support to guide each scout along their unique journeys. By April 2023, Isabelle had simply decided to try something new – to join in the singing, the games, and as a judge for the cooking competition at a Troop 11 campout at Dillon Beach. She was hooked. Jim Crawford-Jakubiak as Troop 11 Assistant Scoutmaster recalls a memorable comment from Isabelle from that trip: “I didn’t realize how fun scouting would be. I wish I [had] joined when I was younger.” Isabelle has definitely made up for lost time, serving in leadership roles including Patrol Leader and Troop Scribe, along her way to earning her Eagle rank. Congratulations to Isabelle Myers, Naomi Treichler, their families, and their respective parent volunteer-driven scouting communities who supported them every single step of the way.

articles.text: One of the strange things about being human is that we can travel hundreds or even thousands of miles to see something interesting, then completely ignore fascinating things that are ten minutes from our front door. When tourists come to town, they often seem to notice things that residents have stopped seeing: a beautiful view from a scenic overlook, a historic building, a quirky local business, a trail, park, or neighborhood that somehow became invisible through familiarity. The irony is that those places did not become less interesting. We simply got used to them. Psychologists call this habituation. The more often we experience something, the less attention we pay to it. It is a remarkably useful feature of the brain because it prevents us from becoming overwhelmed by information. Unfortunately, it can also make us blind to things that are genuinely wonderful. This matters because creativity begins with noticing. Before we create something new, we usually have to see something differently. That is one reason travel can feel so energizing. Everything is unfamiliar. We pay closer attention and notice details. We ask questions and find our curiosity again. But, guess what? Curiosity does not actually require a plane ticket. So here is a summer experiment: spend one afternoon acting like a tourist in your own backyard. Recently, I was taking a walk in my neighborhood and took a turn that I had never taken before. A few minutes into my walk, I passed a home with an absolutely exquisite garden, filled with flowers of all colors. It was stunning and I had never seen it before. So, this summer, visit a place you have never visited. Walk into a store you normally pass by or take a different route on your morning commute. Wander through a neighborhood you’ve never explored. And, most importantly, on your new adventures, bring a tourist’s mindset. Think about the last trip you took, you probably expected to be surprised. But, in your own neighborhood, you expect the predictable. Instead, open yourself to surprise. This experiment is not really about sightseeing –it is about interrupting the assumption that we have already seen everything worth seeing. Because creativity rarely arrives when we are looking at the world on autopilot. It tends to show up when something catches our attention and makes us look twice. This summer, before you plan your next adventure, consider spending a few hours exploring the place where you already are. You might be surprised by how much there is to discover. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/

articles.text: Performances feature famous “Spreckles Organ” Visit Legion of Honor in San Francisco any Saturday afternoon at 4 p.m. and enjoy a free organ concert in the Rodin Gallery by local classically trained organists Jonathan Dimmock, Joy-Leilani Garbutt or Christopher Keady. Dimmock is a graduate of Oberlin and Yale, and the first American to hold the prestigious position of organ scholar of Westminster Abbey. He was resident organist at St. John the Divine in New York City, St. Mark’s in Minneapolis, and Grace Cathedral in San Francisco. Dimmock is principal organist at the Legion of Honor, organist for the San Francisco Symphony, and director of music at Congregation Sherith Israel. He has recorded a Grammy-winning record with the San Francisco Symphony. Garbutt is an organist and cofounder of the Boulanger Initiative, a nonprofit organization that supports female composers. Garbutt spent a year in France researching early 20th-century organ music by female composers exclusively, and currently serves as the director of music for St. Luke’s Episcopal Church in San Francisco. Keady is the interim director of music at the famous Grace Cathedral in San Francisco, where he serves as principal accompanist for the Cathedral Choir of Men and Boys and performs on the cathedral’s Alexander Memorial Organ. Concerts begin at 4 p.m. in Gallery 10 and are free to all museum patrons. All concerts feature the museum’s historic 1924 Skinner pipe organ, called the “Spreckels Organ,” and last approximately 45 minutes to one hour. The concerts are part of the museum’s ongoing dedication to art and music, often featuring a diverse repertoire that complements the surrounding sculptures. The historic “Spreckles Organ” was commissioned by philanthropist John Spreckles and is designed to blend into the museum’s structure. Its 4,500 pipes are not outwardly visible, and the ceiling of the gallery is canvas so that the organ can be heard throughout the gallery and museum. The canvas ceiling is painted as a trompe-l’œil to resemble a marble apse. Residents of all nine Bay Area counties, including Alameda, receive free admission to Legion of Honor in San Francisco on Saturdays. Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano, and Sonoma residents can visit the museum during operating hours and view any of its permanent collection galleries. Visitors ages 17 and under always receive free admission to the permanent collection galleries. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ events/organ-concert to learn more and to register. articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) recently unveiled its newest exhibition, Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs, which explores the evolving dialogue between movement and photography. Feel the Beat, on view now through January 31, 2027, highlights photography’s role in shaping how dance is recorded and remembered, and how dancers have inspired photographers to view movement in a different medium. The new exhibition includes items from SFMOMA’s permanent collection,opening with a gallery devoted to Irving Penn’s images of Anna Halprin and the San Francisco Dancers’ Workshop, as well as pictures that reflect Halprin’s experimental approach to dance. The second gallery turns to Kamaitachi, the partnership between Japanese photographer Eikoh Hosoe and Butoh founder Tatsumi Hijikata. The final section of the exhibition explores ‘nightlife,’ with Malick Sidibé’s Larry Fink, Studio 54, New York City, 1977; on view now at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art photographs of dancing at parties in Mali, as well as photos by Nan Goldin, Larry Fink, Janine Gordon, Weegee, Imogen Cunningham, Barbara Morgan, Robert Rauschenberg, Richard Avedon and more. For more information, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibitions/.
articles.title: Feel the Beat: Dance in Photographs on view now at SFMOMA

articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture (FMCAC) in San Francisco is hosting this month’s Night Market, in partnership with Off the Grid and West Coast Craft, on June 19. The free monthly event in San Francisco runs on select Fridays from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. through December, and features live music, arts and crafts pop-up shops and hands-on workshops, as well as extended hours at nearby museums including Museo Italo Americano and FLAX Art & Design store on select dates. Fort Mason Night Market was conceptualized following the success of an inaugural night market in December that drew over 10,000 attendees. FMCAC hosts outdoor markets once a month through December that transform its iconic campus into a showcase of local artisans, cuisine, and live entertainment. Off the Grid provides more than 25 food and refreshment vendors at each event as attendees enjoy performances by local DJs, engage in hands-on creative workshops, and view public art installations from FMCAC collections. West Coast Craft, founded in San Francisco in 2013 to create a space for independent artists and designers to sell and promote their artwork, is hosted at FMCAC annually and is one of the largest arts fairs in the country. Local artisans who appear at the annual festival, which traditionally takes place in the summer, will be invited to sell their work at monthly Night Market events. “Fort Mason Center is known for being a gathering place, a space for people to exchange ideas, experience beauty, and connect with different modes of art and cultural expressions,” said Mike Buhler, FMCAC’s President and CEO. “We’re excited to collaborate with our partners to offer another way for people to come together, support local arts organizations and small businesses, and enjoy the natural beauty of the campus.” All events are free and open to the public. The next Night Market event will be held on July 24. For more information, visit https://fortmason.org/event/fortmason-night-market-2026/ Live entertainment, arts and food vending take place at the iconic Fort Mason this month.

articles.text: Violinist Pablo de Sarasate Truth is often stranger than fiction. Many famous people claim that they prefer to be “unrecognized“. Incognito might be their nom de plume. While some famous people love being in the spotlight and will do everything they can to gain public attention (think President Trump or boxing champion Muhammad Ali), there are others. You can take this at face value or consider the following stories. They are completely true. Way back in 1895, a friend of mine saw the immortal violinist Pablo de Sarasate sitting in the concert hall of the Milano Conservatory. Sarasate was seated toward the back of the hall on an outside seat with his two Stradivarius violins tucked between his knees. My friend told me that Sarasate had a quiet dignity. What was also interesting is that he always took his instruments with him wherever he went. When speaking of violinists, the name Jascha Heifetz comes to mind. He was a real contradiction. He appreciated being recognized and at the same time he pretended that he enjoyed being incognito. He believed that if he dressed in an “inconspicuous” way, nobody would recognize him. He donned the most outlandish clothing and pulled his hat low over his brow, thinking that he was unrecognizable. Wearing this outlandish outfit to a concert, a friend of mine recognized him and walked over to say hello. My friend asked him, “You are Jascha Heifetz aren’t you?” The man replied, “My name is Joseph.” Both were correct. The man in the outlandish outfit was, in fact Jascha Heifetz. But when the man said that his name was Joseph, this was the truth also.
articles.title: The Musical Gourmet

articles.text: His birth name was actually Joseph Heifetz. He changed the name to Jascha later on. The scene now changes to Manhattan. A music lover recognizes a famous pianist walking in a residential area. The two men began to talk. At the end of the conversation, the music lover said, “Nice to meet you, Mr. Rubenstein.” What a faux pas. The man he had been walking with was famed pianist Vladimir Horowitz – the pianistic enemy of Arthur Rubinstein. We leave the music world for a brief moment, but remain in Manhattan. An older man was going to work as greeter in Jack Dempsey’s restaurant. As he arrived at the front door in a taxi, he was accosted by two muggers. Thinking the old guy was an easy mark, they attacked him. The old guy reacted quickly. He knocked the first mugger out with a left hook, and then knocked the other guy out with a right cross. He then calmly walked into Jack Dempsey‘s restaurant to begin his work as the greeter. I forgot to tell you…the greeter in Jack Dempsey‘s restaurant was the Manassa Mauler himself… Jack Dempsey. Sometimes mistaken identity comes with a knockout punch. Returning to the world of music, we have a very beautiful story involving Paul McCartney of The Beatles. A father was walking in a park with his young daughter at his side. The little girl was an enthusiastic fan of The Beatles, and wouldn’t you know it? Paul McCartney was in that same park. The girl recognized him, and said to him that she loved all of the songs of The Beatles. Paul McCartney asked the little girl what her favorite song was and then he sang it to her. Some things speak for themselves.
articles.title: Incognito

articles.text: Dolly! A Pride Show offers audiences a festive Pride weekend experience. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus launches Pride Month festivities with performances of Dolly! A Pride Show on June 13 at the Curran Theatre in San Francisco, bringing the music of Dolly Parton to the stage in a concert honoring queer joy, resilience and community. Described as a celebration of queer love, chosen family and self-expression, the concert features Parton’s iconic songs reimagined by the chorus. Organized in two acts with an intermission, the program moves from themes of joy and individuality to reflection, solidarity and collective strength. According to organizers, the show draws inspiration from Parton’s long-standing message of kindness, compassion and acceptance. The performance blends camp, humor and heartfelt storytelling while emphasizing the role of joy as a form of resistance and community-building. Founded in 1978, the San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus remains one of the world’s most influential LGBTQ arts organizations. The ensemble was the first openly gay chorus and helped spark a nationwide LGBTQ choral movement following its first public performance at a candlelight vigil on the steps of San Francisco City Hall after the assassinations of Harvey Milk and George Moscone. More than four decades later, the chorus continues to combine artistic excellence with advocacy and community engagement. Dolly! A Pride Show offers audiences a festive Pride weekend experience centered on music, inclusion and the enduring power of belonging. The production will be presented at 1 p.m. and 3 p.m. Tickets are available through the San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus and the Curran Theatre box office websites. Visit https://www.sfgmc.org/ dolly-a-pride-show for more information and to purchase tickets.

He donned the most outlandish clothing and pulled his hat low over his brow, thinking that he was unrecognizable. Wearing this outlandish outfit to a concert, a friend of mine recognized him and walked over to say hello. My friend asked him, “You are Jascha Heifetz aren’t you?” The man replied, “My name is Joseph.” Both were correct. The man in the outlandish outfit was, in fact Jascha Heifetz. But when the man said that his name was Joseph, this was the truth also. His birth name was actually Joseph Heifetz. He changed the name to Jascha later on. The scene now changes to Manhattan. A music lover recognizes a famous pianist walking in a residential area. The two men began to talk. At the end of the conversation, the music lover said, “Nice to meet you, Mr. Rubenstein.” What a faux pas. The man he had been walking with was famed pianist Vladimir Horowitz – the pianistic enemy of Arthur Rubinstein. We leave the music world for a brief moment, but remain in Manhattan. He then calmly walked into Jack Dempsey‘s restaurant to begin his work as the greeter. I forgot to tell you…the greeter in Jack Dempsey‘s restaurant was the Manassa Mauler himself… Jack Dempsey. A father was walking in a park with his young daughter at his side. The little girl was an enthusiastic fan of The Beatles, and wouldn’t you know it? Paul McCartney was in that same park. The girl recognized him, and said to him that she loved all of the songs of The Beatles. Paul McCartney asked the little girl what her favorite song was and then he sang it to her. articles.text: Veus – Cor Infantil Amics de la Unió (Catalonia) Veus – Cor Infantil Amics de la Unió, a youth choir from Catalonia in Spain will be performing this summer at the Golden Gate International Choral Festival hosted by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. It’s spotlight performance is on July 16 at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. It will also participate in the group choral performances on the opening and closing nights of the festival. The choir was founded in 1996 within the Music School created by the Societat Coral Amics de la Unió of Granollers in Barcelona. It is conducted by Josep Vila Jover, who has been with the choir since its formation. The choir stands out for the quality, eclecticism, and uniqueness of its productions. He has been the resident choir director at the Teatre Auditori de Granollers since 2017. Since 1995, Jover has served as the artistic director of the ‘Escola de Música Amics de la Unió,’ a prestigious choral school in Barcelona with over 650 students and 10 active choirs. He is regularly invited to participate in prestigious festivals throughout Europe, notably La Folle Journée (Nantes, France) and Via Aeterna (Mont Saint-Michel, France). In addition the choir has toured and participated in festivals in Japan, China, the United States, and Australia. Veus has participated in numerous international festivals and has been awarded in numerous contests and competitions. Among the most recent awards are the prize for the best interpretation of the obligatory song and the 3rd prize in the children’s category at the 7th Tokyo International Choir Competition (2024), the 3rd prize at the 53rd Toulouse Choral Competition (2022), the prize Josep Anselm Clavé for the best recording for the album Els Colors del Mar (2018), the Guido de Arezzo recognition (2017), the 1st prize at the 47th Toulouse Choral Competition (2015) and the Silver Rose Bowl at the UER Let the Peoples competition Sing! (2013). Veus performs regularly on main stages of the country, such as the Gran Teatre del Liceu (Barcelona), the Palau de la Música Catalana (Barcelona), and the Auditori de Barcelona. Internationally, Jover’s choir has performed at the Philharmonie de Paris and the Philharmonie de Luxembourg. It has shared the stage with prestigious directors such as Kazushi Ono, Jordi Savall, and Gustavo Dudamel. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival, held every three years, takes place this summer from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website https://www.piedmontchoirs. org/ggf-concerts-2026. including which concerts are free for the public.

articles.text: The Family Man and It’s a Wonderful Life rely on the good will nurtured during the Christmas holidays. Yet, at the center of these two exceptional films, replete with wonderful characters and compelling plots, we see that they are not only set in different centuries and vastly different locations (Bedford Falls, N.Y. on the cusp of WWII, and in real time, Wall Street, New York City), both offer contrasting characters: Nicolas Cage as Jack Campbell, a successful Mergers and Acquisitions financier, and James Stewart portraying George Bailey, reluctant heir apparent to a small town Savings and Loan bank. Each narrative asks its audience to suspend its disbelief while managing to find its own comedic sweet spot, while pausing to remind us, in small and large ways, the timeless value of friendship, decency, love and family. Of course, each story relies on two very different angels (Clarence and Cash – portrayed by Henry Travers and Don Cheadle). Both, pushed by unexpected Donna Reed, James Stewart, and Karolyn Grimes in Frank Capra’s It’s a Wonderful Life Tea Leoni and Nicholas Cage in The Family Man events, answer that very human question: “What if?” What if George Bailey’s wish, made in a moment of financial despair, had indeed come true? In response, Clarence takes George on an unsettling tour of Bedford Falls, by way of showing him various unexpected outcomes. Jack Campbell, facing a vastly different moment, tells Cash that he has everything he could ever want. By way of backstory, we see him at the airport, preparing to board a flight bound for England, and he is shown what might have been had he listened to his long-time college girlfriend, Kate Reynolds (Téa Leoni), who asks him not to go. She clearly fears such a separation will change everything going forward. And so it does. But perhaps not. Can life ever offer an extraordinary do-over? An almost magical, transforming, “if only” opportunity in that crossroads moment. Life is about choices. What if we chose wisely, based on unexpected insights and life changing revelations regarding what is truly of value and important? And finally, if a bell rings, remember to answer. No regrets. Happy Father’s Day. The Family Man. Directed by Brett Ratner. Starring Nicolas Cage, Tea Leoni, Don Cheadle. Rated PG-13. 2hrs 5min. articles.text: The Lincoln Lawyer — an episodic series (Seasons 1-5), streaming on several platforms, is a compelling courtroom-drama and legal procedural, based on the bestselling Michael Connelly novels. If you missed the series debut, and if you enjoy a deep dive into a serial character, definitely begin at the beginning and binge-watch, knowing that Seasons 3-4 are ready and good to go. Season 5 has not been released, though Netflix has announced that with the last episode the Lincoln Lawyer saga will wrap. The series has at its center Los Angeles criminal defense attorney Mickey Haller (Manuel Garcia Rulfo), referred to as The Lincoln Lawyer, a moniker derived from his preference to use the backseat of a Lincoln Town Car for his office with a driver, Izzy, an ex-client working off legal fees. His work takes him Manuel Garcia-Rulfo in The Lincoln Lawyer from courthouse hearings, trials, prisons, county jails and client appointments. His assistant, Lorna (Becki Newton), handles all incoming calls, scheduling, and endless paperwork. Each season essentially stands alone with new and carry-over plots, while the core cast returns giving the writers the opportunity to expand in complexity the returning characters. There is Mickey’s extended family and office crew: his first wife, Maggie McPhersone (Neve Campbell), who is an L.A. prosecutor; his investigator, Cisco (Angus Sampson), a rough-edged ex-biker engaged to Lorna (briefly Mickey’s second wife); and his driver, Izzy (Jazz Raycole), a past client,

articles.text: On Monday, June 1, there was a large turnout of 27 members of the First Mondays Reading Group in Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly book discussion. They were there to talk about their June book, Barbarian Days: A Surfing Life by William Finnegan. It won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Biography/Autobiography. This memoir tells the story of Finnegan’s lifelong, obsessive pursuit of surfing from his childhood in California and Hawaii to adventures chasing waves in the South Pacific, Australia, and Africa over the years. The group’s discussion of Barbarian Days reinforced the understanding that a reader’s enjoyment of a book often depends on their prior experiences and ability to connect with its subject matter. While some members found Barbarian Days fascinating and engaging, others found it difficult to relate to and tedious. The conversation underscored how differently the same book can resonate, or not, with different readers. The discussion began spontaneously with members sharing their own surfing and travel experiences, which at times seemed almost more central to the conversation than the book. For several participants, the surfing culture of the 1960s and 1970s had been an important part of their youth. The music of the Beach Boys, surfing magazines, and films such as The Endless Summer were powerful influences. For some, this was a nearly religious experience that shaped their lives. The few members of the group with surfing experience were especially able to relate to the book. They understood the obsession that, for people like Finnegan, bordered on addiction. They had experienced it themselves or witnessed it in friends and family members. Surfing provided a sense of exhilaration, like standing at the edge of a cliff. The bigger the wave, the bigger the thrill. This drive seemed to continue in Finnegan’s later life as he became a war correspondent. It was suggested he was an “adrenaline junkie.” Readers were divided not only about the book itself but also about Finnegan’s writing style. Those who admired it found his descriptions of people, places, and experiences to be vivid, elegant, and often extraordinary. Other readers thought the author’s writing was just “okay” or “good enough.” They liked parts of the book, but lost interest at other times. Readers generally agreed that the second half of the book was better than the first. Throughout the memoir, Finnegan is on both a literal and a figurative journey. His relentless search for the “perfect wave” drives his travels around the world, but surfing is more than a passion; it’s central to his life and identity. At the same time, surfing serves as a vehicle for his personal growth and self-discovery. As the memoir progresses, readers felt Finnegan mature and gain a deeper understanding of himself and his world. Because Barbarian Days is a memoir, its focus naturally remains on Finnegan. However, some readers felt Finnegan lacked self-reflection, and he did not sufficiently present the other people in the book. Several also noted the absence of humor, observing that despite its many adventures and memorable experiences, the book was rarely funny. Personal travel and living in places like Hawaii made some readers more interested in Finnegan’s story. They enjoyed his adventures, people, and the cultures he experienced, but others were looking for more about what Finnegan experienced. He seemed to be an observer but not fully engaged. Surfing always came first. There were also community aspects of Finnegan’s surfing life that readers appreciated. He and his traveling partners, along with other friends, shared a passion that bonded them. While some readers enjoyed, even loved, the book, for others it was a slow “slog.” How many ways could you describe riding Barbarian Days: A Surfing Life by William Finnegan a large wave? They didn’t care about all the surfing minutiae. One reader said her book-skimming skills were helpful to get through this book’s 464 pages. Another reader loved the repetition. It was a way to be a surfer without getting wet. Barbarian Days brought out personal experiences as well as likes and dislikes. The readers agreed they learned about surfing, which may have been more than some wanted, but they were exposed to one man’s obsession and personal growth. Readers agreed that we all have varying degrees of passions, and we hope they lead us to become better people. Future books The readers had previously selected Old Filth by English author Jane Gardam for July and The Art Thief by Michael Finkel for August. After Dick Carter presented three fiction candidates, the group chose Horse by Geraldine Brooks for their September read. With all their business done, they took a group photo outside the Community Hall. The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on July 6 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4. The First Monday Reading group included Bob Hall, Sandy Threlfall, Mary Carter, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Melba Yee, Susan Southworth, Heidi Schmidt, Ken Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Darby Gragg, Tim Weishahn, Susie Backer, Phil Witte, Orrel Lanter, Bill Ahern, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Gerry Gregg, Peggy Shultz, Laura Goldman, Lois Price, Mike Henn, Nadean Guffanti, Sarah Johnson, Odette Pollar, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus.

Further up, they looked across Moraga Avenue to homes on Maxwelton Avenue — one of the few Piedmont streets the group can’t walk to, since there is no sidewalk along busy Moraga. Nancy then led the group to a rustic bungalow at 324 Scenic, once the studio home of painter Marty Martinez. He had built a reputation in Paris in the late 1890s, developing a tonalist style influenced by James McNeill Whistler. He built this house with wine-drinking friends in 1908 and hosted festive parties with bohemian friends, including poet Joaquin Miller. Martinez later moved to Carmel-by-the-Sea, but his daughter, artist Kai Martinez, lived in the home until her death in 1989. The group made its way down the narrow part of Scenic for one more adventure: descending Piedmont’s longest pedestrian pathway, the 281-foot Blair and Scenic Path, whose steep stairs go as far as the eye can see — thankfully with a handrail the entire way. All the walkers got back safely to Blair and, after a round of applause for Nancy’s tour, it was time to party. Nancy then led the group to a rustic bungalow at 324 Scenic, once the studio home of painter Marty Martinez. He had built a reputation in Paris in the late 1890s, developing a tonalist style influenced by James McNeill Whistler. He built this house with wine-drinking friends in 1908 and hosted festive parties with bohemian friends, including poet Joaquin Miller. Martinez later moved to Carmel-by-the-Sea, but his daughter, artist Kai Martinez, lived in the home until her death in 1989. The group made its way down the narrow part of Scenic for one more adventure: descending Piedmont’s longest pedestrian pathway, the 281-foot Blair and Scenic Path, whose steep stairs go as far as the eye can see — thankfully with a handrail the entire way. All the walkers got back safely to Blair and, after a round of applause for Nancy’s tour, it was time to party. They headed down Scenic to the back gate of the DeRoches’ home, where Dave was waiting at his barbecue grill cooking sausages. With a huge birthday cake and plenty of food and drink ready, the appreciative group celebrated Dave and Nancy for over an hour. The first two season plots are all well crafted, and allow Mickey to demonstrate his courtroom skills, style and strategies. The portrayal by Rulfo is excellent as are all the performances. Regarding the season-episodic plots, each flirts with being a somewhat convoluted, but not in a negative way; perhaps challenging is a better word. There’s always an element of “alleged” indictable crimes and a compelling who-dunit mystery. A suggestion: pay close attention. Of course, with streaming, it’s always possible to do a quick playback. It’s hard not to bingewatch the Seasons-episodes once started. If you really want to start at the beginning of what is a creative trifecta plus one, find Michael Connelly’s courtroom novel The Lincoln Lawyer that introduces Mickey Haller. It’s a solid read. Connelly is both an excellent and prolific writer, and able to create a serial character, Harry Bosch, that appeals. He’s the fulcrum in Connelly’s LAPD novels, and is now featured in two Series: Bosch, and Bosch Legacy. Both are set in Los Angeles and are extraordinary examples of the genre. The boys’ team won the WACC Foothill Division title, while the girls’ team shared the WACC title with Bishop O’Dowd. PHS came away with three league titles; the girls’ 4x100 relay team of Akunna Iroh, Aubrecht, Darcy McKee, and Nia Jackson’s victory in the 400 in 49.76 in a field of nine teams, Malia Williams won the high jump in 4 feet, 10 inches against 12 other athletes, while Avedis Gourjian won the pole vault with a height of 12 feet in a field of 10. PHS featured 11 athletes at the NCS Meet of Champions. Aside from Aubrecht, Sebastien Swain placed eighth of 11 in the 800 finals in 2:01.53 and was second of 29 in the prelims in 1:55.45. Uzoma Iroh was 13th of 23 in the shot put in 32 feet, 9 inches, while she was 20th of 24 in the discus in 88 feet, 4 inches. In the high jump, Williams was ninth of 18 athletes with a jump of five feet, while Lucia Dorsey was 13th in 4 feet, 10 inches. Gourjian finished 18th of 23 athletes in the pole vault with a height of 11 feet, 10 inches. Noah Hildebrand was 20th of 22 in the triple jump in 40 feet, 4.25 inches. Saniyah Johnson was 14th in the shot put with a distance of 32 feet, 4 inches. The girls’ 4x400 team of Aubrecht, Skylar Best, Daniela Lucaccini, and Gladwin Horsley finished 21st in 4:28.19. Best placed 22nd of 23 in the 800 prelims in 2:26.23. SWIMMING Peyton Watson finishes her Piedmont career as a four-year varsity member. The boys’ swimming team is in the midst of a renaissance, and things look to continue with another strong team returning in 2027. Piedmont was undefeated during the regular season and dominated the league championship with a collective score of 444 points, beating second-place Berkeley by 39. Aside from the accolades already mentioned at the league championship, Asher Takazawa won the backstroke in 51.15 in a field of 25 swimmers, while Connor Carnazzo won the 100 fly in 50.66 in a field of 26. On the girls’ team, senior leader Sam White won two individual events at the WACC Championships. She won the 200 freestyle in 2:00.86 in a field of 32 swimmers, while she clocked a winning time of 5:23.08 in the 500 free against 20 other athletes.
